title: Address to the Commonwealth Club of California (1984)
author: César Chávez
source: Speech delivered at the Commonwealth Club of California, San Francisco, November 9, 1984
citation: Chávez, César. 'Address to the Commonwealth Club of California.' San Francisco, California, 9 Nov. 1984.

sections.heading: The Reality of Farm Labor in America

epigraph.quote: All my life, I have been driven by one dream, one goal, one vision: to overthrow a farm labor system in this nation that treats farmworkers as if they were not important human beings.

paragraphs: Twenty-two years ago, on a hot September day in Fresno, California, when the United Farm Workers held their first convention, farmworkers were trapped in a cycle of poverty and exploitation that had endured for over a century. We were second-class citizens, forced to live in squalid shacks without running water, denied collective bargaining rights, exposed to lethal pesticides without protective gear, and treated like disposable farm equipment.

The growers and politicians said farmworkers were unorganizable. They said Mexican Americans were too docile, too illiterate, too transient to build a union. But they forgot that hope is stronger than fear, and that human beings will always rise to defend their dignity.

sections.heading: The Nonviolent Weapon of the Consumer Boycott

epigraph.quote: Once social change begins, it cannot be reversed. You cannot un-educate the person who has learned to read. You cannot humiliate the person who feels pride.

paragraphs: Through fasting, nonviolent picketing, and nationwide consumer boycotts of table grapes and lettuce, the United Farm Workers proved that ordinary people could challenge giant agribusiness conglomerates. Millions of American consumers joined hands with farmworkers, refusing to buy grapes until growers signed fair labor contracts providing living wages, health clinics, and pension funds.

Today, although conservative politicians attempt to dismantle our hard-won protections, the true victory cannot be erased. The greatest achievement of the United Farm Workers was not merely financial; it was spiritual. We gave farmworkers a voice, self-respect, and the knowledge that justice is worth fighting for. As I stand here today, I tell you with absolute certainty: our cause is just, our principles are nonviolent, and our victory is inevitable.
